chem_edx.2.0.summary: All matter is made of tiny particles (atoms, molecules or ions), and the three states of matter, solid, liquid and gas, differ only in how those particles are **arranged**, how they **move** and how much **energy** they have. Changing state (melting, freezing, evaporating/boiling, condensing) is a **physical change**: energy is transferred to or from the substance, the forces between particles are overcome or formed, but no new substance is made. Knowing a substance's melting point and boiling point lets you **predict its state** at any temperature.

core.p: The particle model treats every substance as being made of tiny particles that are always moving. The particles of one substance are all the same. The state of the substance depends on how strongly the particles are held together by forces of attraction compared with how much kinetic energy they have.
bullets: Particles can be **atoms**, **molecules** or **ions** depending on the substance
Particles are always moving (even in a solid, where they **vibrate**)
Between particles there are **forces of attraction**
The **stronger** the forces, the more energy is needed to separate particles, so the higher the melting and boiling points
Raising the temperature gives particles more **kinetic energy**, so they move faster
The particles themselves do NOT change size, shape or mass when the state changes

callouts.p: The state of a substance depends on the balance between the **strength of the forces between particles** and the **energy of the particles**.

core.p: In a solid the particles are held very close together in fixed positions by strong forces. They cannot move past each other, which is why solids keep their shape.
bullets: **Arrangement:** particles are touching, in a **regular** pattern (a lattice)
**Movement:** particles only **vibrate** about **fixed positions**
**Energy:** particles have the **least** energy of the three states
Solids have a **fixed shape** and a **fixed volume**
Solids **cannot be compressed** because the particles are already touching
Solids do not flow

core.p: In a liquid the particles are still close together and touching, but the forces are weak enough for them to slide past one another. That is why liquids flow and take the shape of their container.
bullets: **Arrangement:** particles are touching, **random / irregular** arrangement
**Movement:** particles **move around each other** (slide past each other)
**Energy:** particles have **more energy than in a solid** but less than in a gas
Liquids have a **fixed volume** but **no fixed shape** (take the shape of the container)
Liquids **cannot be compressed** (particles are touching)
Liquids flow

callouts.p: A common error is drawing liquid particles widely spaced. In a liquid diagram the particles should be **mostly touching** but randomly arranged.

core.p: In a gas the particles are far apart with almost no forces between them. They move quickly in all directions, so a gas spreads out to fill any container.
bullets: **Arrangement:** particles are **far apart**, **random** arrangement
**Movement:** particles move **quickly** in **random directions** (in straight lines until they collide)
**Energy:** particles have the **most** energy of the three states
Gases have **no fixed shape** and **no fixed volume**: they fill the container
Gases **can be compressed** because there is lots of space between the particles
Gases flow and **diffuse** quickly

core.h: Names of the changes of state
core.p: There are four main interconversions you must name. Each one is reversible, which is one clue that it is a physical change.
bullets: **Melting:** solid to liquid (energy taken in)
**Freezing:** liquid to solid (energy given out)
**Evaporating / boiling:** liquid to gas (energy taken in)
**Condensing:** gas to liquid (energy given out)
**Boiling** happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point; **evaporation** happens only at the surface and can occur below the boiling point
Some substances, e.g. solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) and iodine, go straight from solid to gas: this is **sublimation**

callouts.p: For a pure substance the freezing point and melting point are the **same temperature** (e.g. water: 0 °C). Likewise the condensing point equals the boiling point.

core.h: Changes of state are physical changes
core.p: When a substance changes state, the particles are still the same particles: water molecules in ice, liquid water and steam are all H2O. No new substance is made, so it is a physical change. This is different from a chemical reaction, where atoms are rearranged to make new substances.
bullets: **Physical change:** no new substance formed; usually **easily reversed** (e.g. by heating or cooling)
**Chemical change:** **new substance(s)** formed; bonds within particles broken and made; usually hard to reverse
Mass is **conserved** during a change of state (same particles, same number)
Signs of a chemical change: colour change not due to state, gas given off from a reaction, new product with different properties, energy change that is not just a change of state
Example of a physical change: ice melting; example of a chemical change: burning magnesium to make magnesium oxide

callouts.p: A change in which **no new substance is made**; the particles stay the same and the change can usually be reversed.

core.h: Explaining melting and boiling with energy
core.p: Heating transfers energy to the particles. In a solid this makes them vibrate more. At the melting point the particles have enough energy to **overcome some of the forces of attraction** holding them in fixed positions, so they can move around each other: the solid melts. At the boiling point particles have enough energy to **overcome the remaining forces** and escape into the gas.
bullets: Energy must be **transferred to** the substance to melt or boil it
The energy is used to **overcome the forces of attraction between particles**, not to break the particles apart
Stronger forces between particles mean **more energy** is needed, so the melting / boiling point is **higher**
Boiling needs more energy than melting because the particles must be separated completely, not just loosened
Evaporation below the boiling point: the most energetic particles at the surface escape, so the liquid left behind cools

callouts.t: Do not say bonds break inside molecules
callouts.p: For a simple molecular substance like water, boiling overcomes the **forces between molecules**. The covalent bonds inside each H2O molecule are NOT broken. Saying 'covalent bonds break' loses the mark.

core.p: Cooling is the reverse. As the gas cools, particles lose kinetic energy and move more slowly. Attractive forces can then pull them together into a liquid (condensing). Further cooling lets the forces hold the particles in fixed positions (freezing). Energy is transferred from the substance to the surroundings as the forces form.
bullets: Energy is **transferred to the surroundings** during condensing and freezing
Particles **slow down** and come closer together
Forces of attraction between the particles **pull them together** / hold them in place
Condensation on a cold window: water vapour particles lose energy to the cold glass and become liquid

core.p: If you heat a pure solid steadily and record the temperature, the graph has flat sections. During a flat section the substance is changing state: the energy supplied is being used to overcome forces between particles rather than to increase the kinetic energy of the particles, so the temperature stays constant.
bullets: **Sloping sections:** only one state present; temperature rises as particles gain kinetic energy
**First flat section:** melting (solid and liquid both present) at the **melting point**
**Second flat section:** boiling (liquid and gas present) at the **boiling point**
The boiling plateau is usually **longer** because more energy is needed to separate the particles completely
A **cooling curve** is the mirror image: flat sections at the boiling (condensing) point and the melting (freezing) point, where energy is released as forces form
A **pure** substance has a flat plateau at one exact temperature

callouts.p: During a change of state the energy supplied is used to **overcome the forces of attraction between particles**, so the particles' kinetic energy (and so the temperature) does not increase.

core.p: To predict the state of a substance at a given temperature, compare that temperature with the substance's melting point and boiling point.
bullets: Temperature **below the melting point**: **solid**
Temperature **between the melting point and the boiling point**: **liquid**
Temperature **above the boiling point**: **gas**
Room temperature is usually taken as **20 or 25 °C**
Watch negative numbers: -10 °C is higher than -50 °C
At exactly the melting point the substance could be solid, liquid or both (changing state)

callouts.p: Sketch a quick line with the m.p. and b.p. marked, then place the temperature on it. It stops mistakes with negative numbers.

core.p: The simple model is very useful but it is not a perfect picture of reality. Higher-scoring answers can say what it leaves out.
bullets: Particles are drawn as **solid spheres**, but real atoms and molecules are not hard balls and have different shapes
It does **not show the forces** between the particles
It suggests all particles are the **same size**, which is not true for every substance
Diagrams are **2D** but real substances are **3D**
Gas particles are shown far too close; in reality the spaces are much bigger compared with particle size
Particles in diagrams appear still; in reality they are always moving

analogy.p: A **solid** is a class sitting in rows during an exam: packed close, in fixed seats, only fidgeting (vibrating). A **liquid** is the same students in a crowded corridor at break: still bumping into each other but sliding past one another and moving around. A **gas** is everyone on the field at lunch: spread far apart, running fast in random directions. The bell ringing (heating) gives them energy to break out of their fixed positions. Where it breaks down: students choose to move and have different sizes, whereas particles of one substance are identical and move only because of their energy; and students do not have forces of attraction pulling them together.

terms.d: A tiny piece of matter, which can be an atom, a molecule or an ion.
A model that explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases in terms of the arrangement, movement and energy of particles.
State in which particles are touching in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions; lowest energy.
State in which particles are touching in a random arrangement and move around each other.
State in which particles are far apart in a random arrangement and move quickly in all directions; highest energy.
The change of state from solid to liquid; energy is taken in.
The change of state from liquid to solid; energy is given out.
The change from liquid to gas that happens at the surface of a liquid, at temperatures below the boiling point.
The change from liquid to gas that happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.
The change of state from gas to liquid; energy is given out.
The change directly from solid to gas without becoming a liquid, e.g. dry ice.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid (the same temperature at which the liquid freezes).
The temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into a gas throughout its volume.
A change in which no new substance is made, such as a change of state; usually easily reversed.
A change in which one or more new substances are formed, as in a chemical reaction.
The forces between particles that hold them together; they must be overcome to melt or boil a substance.
The energy a particle has because it is moving; it increases as temperature increases.

mistakes.w: In a liquid the particles are spread out.
mistakes.r: In a liquid the particles are close together / touching but randomly arranged.

mistakes.w: Particles in a solid do not move.
mistakes.r: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions.

mistakes.w: Particles expand when a substance is heated.
mistakes.r: The particles stay the same size; they gain energy and move faster / further apart.

mistakes.w: When water boils, the bonds in the water molecules break.
mistakes.r: The forces of attraction between the water molecules are overcome; covalent bonds inside molecules do not break.

mistakes.w: Melting is a chemical change because it needs energy.
mistakes.r: Melting is a physical change: no new substance is formed and it is easily reversed.

mistakes.w: The temperature stays the same on the plateau because no energy is being supplied.
mistakes.r: Energy is still supplied but it is used to overcome forces between particles, not to increase kinetic energy.

mistakes.w: A substance with m.p. -7 °C and b.p. 59 °C is a gas at 25 °C because 25 is above -7.
mistakes.r: 25 °C is between the melting and boiling points, so it is a liquid.

mistakes.w: Evaporating and boiling are the same thing.
mistakes.r: Boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point; evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature below it.

mistakes.w: Condensing takes in energy.
mistakes.r: Condensing and freezing transfer energy to the surroundings (energy given out).

exam.q: Name the change of state when a gas turns into a liquid.
model: Condensing / condensation
exam.tip: Spell it correctly and do not confuse it with freezing.

exam.q: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a solid.
model: Particles touching / close together in a regular arrangement
Particles vibrate about fixed positions
exam.tip: One mark for arrangement, one for movement: always give both.

exam.q: Draw diagrams to show the arrangement of particles in a liquid and in a gas.
model: Liquid: at least 5 particles, mostly touching, random arrangement
Gas: at least 5 particles, widely spaced, random arrangement, none touching
exam.tip: Draw particles the same size in both boxes.

exam.q: Bromine has a melting point of -7 °C and a boiling point of 59 °C. Predict its state at 25 °C and at 80 °C.
model: 25 °C: liquid (between m.p. and b.p.)
80 °C: gas (above b.p.)
exam.tip: Give a reason using the m.p. and b.p. if the question says explain.

exam.q: State why the melting of ice is a physical change, not a chemical change.
model: No new substance is formed (it is still water / H2O) / it is easily reversed
exam.tip: 'No new substance' is the key phrase.

exam.q: Explain why a gas can be compressed but a liquid cannot.
model: In a gas the particles are far apart / there are large spaces between them
In a liquid the particles are touching so cannot be pushed closer together
exam.tip: Compare both states for both marks.

exam.q: Compare the relative energy of the particles in the three states of matter.
model: Gas particles have the most energy, solid particles the least
Liquid particles have more energy than solid but less than gas
exam.tip: The spec uses the phrase 'relative energy': give an order.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of particles, what happens when a solid is heated until it melts.
model: Energy is transferred to the particles / particles gain kinetic energy
Particles vibrate more / faster
At the melting point particles have enough energy to overcome some forces of attraction
Particles can then move around each other / leave fixed positions, so solid becomes liquid
exam.tip: Use the word 'overcome' and refer to forces BETWEEN particles.

exam.q: A pure substance is heated at a steady rate. Explain why the temperature stays constant while it boils.
model: Energy supplied is used to overcome the forces between the particles
So the kinetic energy of the particles / temperature does not increase
exam.tip: Never say no energy is being supplied.

exam.q: Explain why boiling needs more energy than melting for the same substance.
model: When melting, only some of the forces between particles are overcome / particles stay touching
When boiling, (all) the remaining forces must be overcome so particles separate completely / move far apart
exam.tip: Link to the longer boiling plateau on a heating curve.

exam.q: Describe and explain the changes to the particles of a substance as it is cooled from a gas at 150 °C to a solid at -20 °C. The substance has m.p. 5 °C and b.p. 80 °C.
model: At 150 °C it is a gas: particles far apart, random, moving quickly
As it cools, particles lose (kinetic) energy and slow down
At 80 °C it condenses: forces of attraction pull particles together into a liquid; energy given out
Between 80 °C and 5 °C liquid: particles touching, random, move around each other
At 5 °C it freezes: particles held in fixed positions in a regular arrangement; energy given out
Temperature stays constant during each change of state; at -20 °C it is a solid in which particles only vibrate
exam.tip: Work through in order of temperature and name each change of state at its temperature.

worked.q: Use the data to state the physical state of each substance at 20 °C: A (m.p. -95 °C, b.p. 69 °C), B (m.p. 1083 °C, b.p. 2567 °C), C (m.p. -210 °C, b.p. -196 °C).
steps: Rule: below m.p. = solid; between m.p. and b.p. = liquid; above b.p. = gas
A: 20 is above -95 but below 69, so between m.p. and b.p.
B: 20 is below 1083, so below m.p.
C: 20 is above -196, so above b.p.
worked.ans: A is a liquid, B is a solid, C is a gas.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why water vapour condenses on a cold window.
steps: Water vapour is a gas: particles far apart, moving fast
When the particles hit the cold glass they transfer energy to it and slow down
With less kinetic energy the forces of attraction can pull the particles together
The particles become close together / touching and random: a liquid forms
This is a physical change: the substance is still water
worked.ans: Water particles lose energy to the cold glass, slow down, and attractive forces pull them close together so the gas condenses to liquid water.

worked.q: A student heats a solid at a steady rate. The temperature rises to 54 °C, stays at 54 °C for 3 minutes, then rises again. Explain what is happening during the 3 minutes.
steps: The flat part shows a change of state at constant temperature
54 °C is the melting point, so the solid is melting
Both solid and liquid are present
Energy is still being supplied but is used to overcome forces of attraction between particles
So the kinetic energy of the particles, and the temperature, do not rise
worked.ans: The substance is melting at its melting point of 54 °C; energy supplied overcomes the forces between particles, so the temperature stays constant.

chem_edx.2.1.summary: In everyday language 'pure' means natural or has had nothing added, but in chemistry a **pure substance** is a single element or a single compound, not mixed with anything else. A **mixture** contains two or more substances that are not chemically joined, so they keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods. The best test of purity is the **melting point**: a pure substance melts at a **sharp, fixed temperature**, while a mixture (impure substance) melts over a **range of temperatures**, usually lower than the pure substance.

core.h: 'Pure' in everyday life vs in chemistry
core.p: Food labels say things like 'pure orange juice' or 'pure spring water'. This everyday meaning is 'natural' or 'nothing artificial added'. But orange juice contains water, sugars, acids and many other substances, and spring water contains dissolved minerals, so to a chemist they are mixtures.
bullets: **Everyday use:** pure means a natural substance that has not had anything added to it / is unprocessed
**Chemistry use:** pure means a **single element or a single compound**, not mixed with any other substance
'Pure' milk, 'pure' honey and 'pure' fruit juice are all **mixtures** in chemistry
Bottled mineral water is a mixture of water and dissolved salts
Pure water in chemistry contains only H2O molecules, e.g. **distilled water**

callouts.p: A **single element or a single compound**, not mixed with any other substance.

core.p: An element is made of only one type of atom. A compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. If a sample contains only one element or only one compound, it is pure.
bullets: **Element:** only one type of atom, e.g. oxygen O2, iron Fe, helium He
**Compound:** two or more different elements **chemically bonded** in a **fixed ratio**, e.g. water H2O, sodium chloride NaCl, carbon dioxide CO2
A compound has a fixed composition and so a fixed set of properties (e.g. melting point)
A compound's properties are different from those of the elements it is made from (sodium is a reactive metal, chlorine a toxic gas, sodium chloride is table salt)
Compounds can only be separated into their elements by a **chemical reaction**, not by physical methods

core.p: A mixture contains two or more different substances (elements and/or compounds) that are **not chemically combined**. Because the substances are not bonded to each other, each keeps its own properties.
bullets: Components are **not chemically joined**
Each component **keeps its own properties** (e.g. iron in an iron and sulfur mixture is still magnetic)
The **proportions can vary** (you can add more salt to salt water)
Mixtures can be separated by **physical methods**: filtration, crystallisation, distillation, chromatography
Examples: air, sea water, crude oil, ink, alloys such as steel, salt solution
A mixture does not have a single fixed melting point or boiling point

callouts.p: Two or more substances (elements or compounds) that are **not chemically combined** together.

core.h: Why melting point is a test of purity
core.p: Every pure substance has its own **fixed, sharp melting point** under standard conditions, for example pure water melts at exactly 0 °C. Because all the particles are identical, the forces between them are all the same, so they all need the same energy to overcome them and the whole sample melts at one temperature.
bullets: **Pure substance:** melts at a **sharp / specific / fixed** temperature
**Impure substance (mixture):** melts over a **range of temperatures**
Impurities usually **lower** the melting point (and **raise** the boiling point)
Impurity particles disrupt the regular arrangement of particles, so the forces are not all the same and some parts melt before others
The more impurity present, the **lower** the melting point and the **wider** the melting range
You can identify a pure substance by comparing its measured melting point with a **data book value**

callouts.p: **Pure = sharp melting point. Mixture = melts over a range of temperatures.**

core.p: Exam questions give you melting point data and ask whether a sample is pure. Look at two things: is it a single sharp value, and does it match the known value for the pure substance?
bullets: A **single value** that **matches the data book** value: sample is pure
A **range** (e.g. 118-123 °C): sample is a mixture / impure
A value **lower** than the data book value: impure
A narrower range closer to the true value suggests a purer sample
Two samples with the same sharp melting point are likely the same pure substance
Example: pure aspirin melts at 136 °C; a sample melting at 128-133 °C is impure

callouts.p: In 'explain' questions quote the numbers, e.g. 'sample B melts over a range from 128 to 133 °C, below 136 °C, so it is impure'.

core.h: Heating curves for pure and impure substances
core.p: If you heat a solid at a steady rate and plot temperature against time, a pure substance gives a **flat plateau** at its melting point. A mixture gives a **sloping section** instead, because it melts gradually over a range of temperatures.
bullets: Pure: horizontal line at the melting point
Mixture: gentle slope that starts at a lower temperature
Cooling curves show the same pattern for freezing points
Plateau = energy used to overcome forces between particles rather than raising temperature

fig.cap: Heating curves. The pure substance (red) has a flat plateau at one temperature: a sharp melting point. The impure substance (blue) melts over a range of temperatures that starts lower, so the line slopes.

core.p: A small amount of the dry, powdered solid is put into a thin glass capillary tube. The tube is heated slowly next to a thermometer, either in an electric melting point apparatus or in a beaker of oil or water. You record the temperature when the solid starts to melt and when it has completely melted.
bullets: Make sure the solid is **dry** (water is an impurity)
Use a **small amount** packed at the bottom of a **capillary tube**
Heat **slowly**, especially near the expected melting point, so the thermometer reading keeps up with the sample
Record the temperature at which melting **starts** and the temperature at which it **finishes**
A small gap between these two values means the sample is pure
Stir the oil / water bath so the temperature is even

callouts.p: If you heat too quickly the thermometer reading lags behind, so the recorded melting point and range are inaccurate.

core.p: Boiling point can also show purity. A pure liquid boils at a fixed temperature (pure water at 100 °C at normal pressure). Dissolved impurities raise the boiling point and make the liquid boil over a range.
bullets: Sea water boils above 100 °C because of the dissolved salts
Boiling point also depends on air pressure, so melting point is the more common test
A pure liquid distilling over at a constant temperature indicates a pure distillate

core.p: In industries such as medicines, food and electronics, impurities can be harmful or can stop a product working. Checking the melting point is a quick, cheap quality check.
bullets: Medicines must be pure because impurities could be toxic or change the dose
Food additives and flavourings must meet purity standards
A chemist making a new compound checks its melting point to see if purification (e.g. recrystallisation) worked

core.p: Some useful products are deliberately made as mixtures with carefully measured amounts of each component, called formulations. They are not pure, but they are designed to have particular properties.
bullets: Examples: paints, medicines (tablets), fertilisers, alloys, cleaning products
Each component has a specific purpose and is in a measured quantity
A formulation will melt over a range, as it is a mixture

core.h: Grade 9 explanation: why impurities widen the melting range
core.p: In a pure solid the particles are identical and packed in a regular pattern, so the forces between them are all equal and are overcome at a single temperature. Impurity particles are a different size and disrupt the pattern. This weakens some of the forces, so parts of the solid begin to melt at a lower temperature, and the sample melts gradually as it is heated.
bullets: Identical particles + identical forces = one sharp melting point
Different particles disrupt the regular lattice
Weaker / uneven forces = melting starts lower and spreads over a range
More impurity = bigger effect

callouts.p: For 'explain' questions link the observation (sharp vs range) to the **particles** (identical vs different) and the **forces** between them.

analogy.p: A pure substance is like a choir in which every singer is the same and they all hit the note at the same instant: everything happens at one exact moment (one sharp melting point). Add some singers who learned a slightly different version (impurities) and the choir comes in raggedly over a few seconds, starting a little early (melting over a range, starting lower). Where it breaks down: singers choose when to sing, while particles melt only because of the energy they have and the forces between them; and real impurities lower the melting point for physical reasons, not because they are 'early'.

terms.d: A single element or a single compound, not mixed with any other substance.
A natural substance that has had nothing added to it; may still be a mixture chemically.
A substance made of only one type of atom.
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
Two or more substances that are not chemically combined; each keeps its own properties.
An unwanted substance mixed with the substance you want.
A substance containing other substances mixed with it; it is a mixture.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
Melting at one specific, fixed temperature; shows the substance is pure.
The range of temperatures over which a mixture melts, from where melting starts to where it finishes.
The temperature at which a liquid boils; raised by dissolved impurities.
A way of separating a mixture without a chemical reaction, e.g. filtration, distillation, chromatography.
The accepted melting or boiling point of the pure substance, used for comparison.
A mixture designed as a useful product, with each component in a measured quantity.
A thin glass tube that holds a small solid sample when measuring its melting point.

mistakes.w: Pure orange juice is a pure substance.
mistakes.r: Orange juice is a mixture of many substances; 'pure' here only has its everyday meaning.

mistakes.w: A pure substance has a high melting point.
mistakes.r: A pure substance has a sharp / fixed melting point (it can be high or low).

mistakes.w: An impure substance has a higher melting point.
mistakes.r: Impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.

mistakes.w: Mineral water is pure because nothing is added.
mistakes.r: It contains dissolved minerals / salts, so it is a mixture.

mistakes.w: A mixture is when elements are bonded together.
mistakes.r: In a mixture the substances are not chemically combined; bonded elements make a compound.

mistakes.w: A compound is impure because it contains more than one element.
mistakes.r: A compound is a pure substance: one substance with a fixed composition.

mistakes.w: The sample is impure because it melts at 80 °C.
mistakes.r: Compare with the data value and look for a range: impure if it melts over a range or below the expected value.

mistakes.w: Mixtures can only be separated by chemical reactions.
mistakes.r: Mixtures can be separated by physical methods; compounds need chemical reactions.

exam.q: State the meaning of the word 'pure' in chemistry.
model: A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance
exam.tip: Say 'single substance' or 'element or compound' and 'not mixed'.

exam.q: A carton is labelled 'pure apple juice'. Explain why a chemist would not describe it as pure.
model: Apple juice contains several / many different substances (e.g. water, sugars, acids)
So it is a mixture, not a single substance
exam.tip: Contrast everyday meaning with chemical meaning.

exam.q: State what is meant by a mixture.
model: Two or more substances (elements or compounds) not chemically combined
exam.tip: The key words are 'not chemically combined'.

exam.q: Describe how the melting of a pure substance differs from the melting of a mixture.
model: A pure substance melts at a sharp / fixed / specific temperature
A mixture melts over a range of temperatures
exam.tip: You can add that the mixture's range is usually lower.

exam.q: Pure stearic acid melts at 69 °C. Sample X melts between 64 °C and 67 °C. Explain what this shows.
model: X is impure / a mixture
because it melts over a range and below 69 °C
exam.tip: Quote the data to back up the conclusion.

exam.q: Which of these is a pure substance? A air B sea water C distilled water D steel
model: C distilled water
exam.tip: Steel is an alloy: a mixture.

exam.q: Give two differences between a compound and a mixture.
model: Compound: elements chemically combined; mixture: substances not chemically combined
Compound has a fixed composition / mixture's proportions can vary / compound separated only by chemical reaction, mixture by physical methods
exam.tip: Write each difference as a comparison.

exam.q: Explain why a pure substance has a sharp melting point.
model: All the particles are the same, so the forces between them are the same
So the same energy is needed to overcome them and they all melt at one temperature
exam.tip: Talk about particles and forces, not just 'it is pure'.

exam.q: Describe how a student could measure the melting point of a solid to check whether it is pure.
model: Put a small amount of dry, powdered solid in a capillary tube
Place it next to a thermometer in a melting point apparatus / oil bath
Heat slowly and record the temperatures when it starts and finishes melting
Compare with data book value: sharp and matching = pure; range / lower = impure
exam.tip: Remember 'heat slowly' and 'compare with data book value'.

exam.q: A student makes aspirin and wants to know how pure it is. Explain how melting point data could be used, and describe what results would show a pure and an impure product.
model: Measure the melting point of the product using a melting point apparatus / capillary tube
Heat slowly and record the start and end of melting
Compare with the data book value for pure aspirin
Pure: melts at a sharp temperature that matches the data book value
Impure: melts over a range of temperatures
Impure: melting point lower than the data value; a wider range / bigger drop means more impurity
exam.tip: For 6 marks cover method, comparison, and both outcomes with reasons.

worked.q: Pure naphthalene melts at 80 °C. Four samples gave: P 80 °C, Q 74-78 °C, R 79-80 °C, S 70-76 °C. Rank them from most to least pure.
steps: Pure substances melt at a sharp temperature matching the data value
P melts at exactly 80 °C: pure
R has a narrow 1 °C range just below 80 °C: almost pure
Q has a 4 °C range starting at 74 °C
S has a 6 °C range starting at 70 °C: widest range and lowest, so most impure
worked.ans: P > R > Q > S (most pure to least pure).

worked.q: Classify each as a pure substance or a mixture: oxygen gas, salt solution, carbon dioxide, brass, 'pure' honey.
steps: Oxygen: only one element (O2 molecules): pure
Salt solution: salt dissolved in water, not bonded: mixture
Carbon dioxide: one compound, CO2: pure
Brass: alloy of copper and zinc: mixture
Honey: sugars, water and other substances: mixture (only 'pure' in everyday sense)
worked.ans: Pure: oxygen, carbon dioxide. Mixtures: salt solution, brass, honey.

chem_edx.2.2.summary: Because the substances in a mixture are not chemically joined, they can be separated by **physical methods** that exploit differences in their properties: **solubility**, **particle state** and **boiling point**. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; crystallisation gets a soluble solid out of its solution; simple distillation separates a liquid from a solution; fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with different boiling points; and paper chromatography separates soluble substances such as dyes. At grade 9 you must be able to **choose and justify** the right method (or sequence of methods) from the properties of the components.

core.h: Why mixtures can be separated physically
core.p: In a mixture each substance keeps its own properties. If two substances differ in a property, such as whether they dissolve or the temperature at which they boil, we can use that difference to pull them apart without any chemical reaction.
bullets: **Solubility** difference: filtration (insoluble vs soluble / liquid)
Dissolved solid vs solvent: **crystallisation** (keep the solid) or **simple distillation** (keep the liquid)
**Boiling point** difference between liquids: **fractional distillation**
Different **solubility in a solvent / attraction to paper**: **paper chromatography**
No new substances are made, so these are **physical** processes

callouts.p: Always name the **property** that is different and say how the method uses it.

core.p: Filtration separates an **insoluble solid** from a **liquid** (or solution). The filter paper has tiny holes: liquid particles and dissolved particles are small enough to pass through, but the larger solid grains are trapped.
bullets: Use: insoluble solid from liquid, e.g. **sand from salt solution**, excess insoluble base from a salt solution, a precipitate from a solution
Fold filter paper into a cone and place it in a **filter funnel** over a beaker or conical flask
Pour the mixture in slowly; do not overfill above the top of the paper
**Residue:** the solid left in the filter paper
**Filtrate:** the liquid / solution that passes through
Wash the residue with a little distilled water to remove traces of solution, then dry it

callouts.p: **Filtrate** = the liquid that passes through the filter paper. **Residue** = the insoluble solid left behind in the filter paper.

fig.cap: Filtration. The insoluble solid (residue) is trapped by the filter paper; the liquid or solution (filtrate) passes through into the flask.

core.p: Crystallisation obtains a **soluble solid** from a **solution**, for example salt crystals from salt solution or copper sulfate crystals from copper sulfate solution. The solvent is partly evaporated so the solution becomes more concentrated, then it is left to cool so crystals form.
bullets: Pour the solution into an **evaporating basin**
Heat gently (over a water bath or on a gauze) to evaporate **some** of the water
Stop when the solution is **saturated**: crystals start to form at the edge, or form on a cold glass rod dipped in and removed
Leave the solution to **cool slowly**; the solid is less soluble when cold, so **crystals form**
**Filter** off the crystals and **dry** them between filter papers or in a warm oven
Slow cooling gives **larger** crystals

callouts.p: Heating until all the water has gone can make the solid **spit** out of the basin and can **decompose** some salts (e.g. hydrated salts lose their water of crystallisation). It also leaves soluble impurities mixed in with the product.

core.p: Simple distillation separates a **liquid (solvent) from a solution**, for example pure water from salt solution or ink. The solution is heated so the solvent boils; its vapour rises, passes into a cooled condenser, condenses back to a liquid and drips into a beaker. The dissolved solid has a much higher boiling point, so it stays behind in the flask.
bullets: Heat the solution in a flask (add **anti-bumping granules** for smooth boiling)
The solvent **evaporates / boils**; the solute stays behind
The **thermometer bulb** is level with the side arm so it measures the temperature of the vapour leaving the flask
The **condenser** has cold water flowing in at the **bottom** and out at the **top**, so the jacket stays full and cooling is most effective
Vapour **condenses** in the cold condenser and the pure liquid collects as the **distillate**
A steady thermometer reading at the boiling point (e.g. 100 °C for water) shows a pure distillate

callouts.t: Why water enters at the bottom
callouts.p: Water in at the bottom fills the condenser completely and flows against the vapour (counter-current), giving the best cooling.

core.p: Fractional distillation separates a mixture of **miscible liquids** (liquids that mix) that have **different boiling points**, for example ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) and water (b.p. 100 °C), or the fractions in crude oil. A **fractionating column** above the flask is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. Vapours rise up the column; the liquid with the higher boiling point condenses on the glass beads and drips back, while the liquid with the lowest boiling point reaches the top and passes into the condenser first.
bullets: Use when the liquids are **miscible** and their boiling points are **close** (simple distillation would not separate them well)
The column has a **temperature gradient**: hot at the bottom, cooler at the top
Glass beads / rods give a **large surface area** for repeated evaporation and condensation
The liquid with the **lowest boiling point** distils over **first**
The thermometer reading stays steady while one liquid distils, then **rises** when the next liquid starts to come over
Change the collecting beaker when the temperature rises to collect each **fraction** separately
Used industrially to separate **crude oil** and liquefied air

callouts.p: Simple distillation: **solvent from a solution** (big difference in boiling point). Fractional distillation: **liquids from each other** with different, often close, boiling points.

core.p: Paper chromatography separates **soluble substances** in a mixture, for example the different dyes in an ink or food colouring. A spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil line on chromatography paper, and the bottom of the paper is dipped in a solvent. As the solvent moves up the paper it carries the substances different distances, depending on how soluble they are in the solvent and how strongly they are attracted to the paper.
bullets: Use: separating and identifying **dyes, inks, food colourings**
**Stationary phase:** the paper; **mobile phase:** the solvent
More soluble substances / less attracted to paper travel **further**
Draw the start line in **pencil** (ink would dissolve and run)
Solvent level must be **below** the start line, or the spots dissolve into the solvent
Place a lid on the container so the paper is surrounded by solvent vapour
Details of chromatograms and Rf values are covered in points 2.9-2.10

core.p: Both remove the solvent to leave the dissolved solid, but they are not the same. Evaporation to dryness is quick but can damage the product; crystallisation is slower but gives purer, well-formed crystals.
bullets: **Evaporation to dryness:** heat until all the solvent has gone; fast, but salts may decompose and soluble impurities remain
**Crystallisation:** evaporate only some solvent, then cool; crystals form, impurities mostly stay dissolved in the remaining solution
Choose crystallisation when the salt is **hydrated** or decomposes on strong heating (e.g. copper sulfate)

core.h: Choosing a method: the decision table
core.p: To choose a method, think about what each component is (solid or liquid), whether it is soluble, and which component you want to keep.
bullets: **Insoluble solid + liquid** -> filtration
**Soluble solid dissolved in liquid, want the solid** -> crystallisation
**Soluble solid dissolved in liquid, want the liquid** -> simple distillation
**Two or more miscible liquids, different boiling points** -> fractional distillation
**Several soluble coloured substances / dyes** -> paper chromatography
**Mixture of soluble and insoluble solids** -> add water, stir, filter (insoluble stays as residue), then crystallise the filtrate

head: Mixture
Property used
Method
Example
rows: Solvent evaporates; less soluble when cool
Solubility in solvent / attraction to paper

callouts.p: Marks come from linking the method to a property, e.g. 'filter because sand is **insoluble** in water'.

core.p: Real mixtures often need more than one method in sequence. Plan each step from the properties of every component.
bullets: **Rock salt (salt + sand):** grind, add warm water and stir to dissolve the salt; filter to remove sand (residue); crystallise salt from the filtrate
**Sand, salt and water, keep the water too:** filter out sand, then simply distil the filtrate to collect water and leave salt
**Iron filings + sand + salt:** use a magnet for iron, then dissolve, filter and crystallise
**Excess insoluble reactant in a salt preparation:** filter off the excess, then crystallise the salt from the filtrate

core.p: Examiners often ask for a safety precaution or an improvement to the method.
bullets: Wear **eye protection**: hot solutions can spit
Use **anti-bumping granules** in distillation so the liquid boils smoothly
Heat flammable liquids such as ethanol with an **electric heater or water bath**, not a naked flame
Do not heat a sealed apparatus: the distillation set-up must be **open** at the collecting end
Never let the flask boil dry
Do not let the water flow out of the condenser stop, or vapour will escape uncondensed

callouts.p: In distillation the thermometer bulb goes **at the side arm / top of the column**, not in the liquid: it measures the boiling point of the vapour being collected.

core.h: Grade 9 reasoning: why fractional distillation works
core.p: In the column, vapour of both liquids rises. As it meets the cooler beads, the substance with the higher boiling point condenses more easily and runs back down, while the lower boiling point substance stays as vapour. This evaporate-condense cycle repeats many times up the column, so the vapour becomes richer in the lower boiling point liquid at each stage. By the top, almost pure vapour of the lowest boiling point component leaves the column.
bullets: Many repeated evaporations and condensations = many 'mini distillations'
Bigger surface area (beads) and a longer column give better separation
When the first liquid has gone, the temperature at the top rises to the next boiling point

analogy.t: Sorting a school bag at the end of term
analogy.p: Filtration is a sieve: big things (insoluble grains) are caught, small things (water and dissolved particles) fall through. Crystallisation is letting a puddle of sugary drink dry slowly until the sugar is left behind. Distillation is like a lift that only takes passengers who are 'light enough' (low boiling point) up to a new floor; heavier ones stay below. Fractional distillation is a tall building with many floors getting colder as you go up: each floor sends the heavier passengers back down until only the lightest reach the top. Where it breaks down: particles in filtration are separated by size of grains, not individual particle size, and in distillation the deciding factor is the strength of forces between particles (boiling point), not mass alone.

mistakes.w: Use filtration to separate salt from salt water.
mistakes.r: Salt is dissolved, so it passes through filter paper; use crystallisation (or distillation to collect the water).

mistakes.w: Use simple distillation to separate ethanol and water.
mistakes.r: They are miscible with fairly close boiling points; use fractional distillation.

mistakes.w: Heat the salt solution until all the water has evaporated.
mistakes.r: Heat to evaporate some water until crystals start to form, then leave to cool and crystallise.

mistakes.w: Cold water enters the condenser at the top.
mistakes.r: Water enters at the bottom and leaves at the top so the condenser stays full and cools efficiently.

mistakes.w: The thermometer goes in the boiling liquid.
mistakes.r: The thermometer bulb is at the side arm / top of the column to measure the vapour temperature.

mistakes.w: The liquid with the highest boiling point comes off first.
mistakes.r: The liquid with the lowest boiling point distils first.

mistakes.w: Filtration works because the liquid is lighter than the solid.
mistakes.r: Filtration works because the solid is insoluble and its grains are too large to pass through the paper.

mistakes.w: The filtrate is the solid in the filter paper.
mistakes.r: The solid in the paper is the residue; the filtrate is the liquid that passes through.

mistakes.w: Draw the chromatography start line in pen.
mistakes.r: Use pencil, because ink would dissolve in the solvent and separate.

exam.q: Name the method used to separate sand from water.
model: Filtration
exam.tip: One-word answer, spelled correctly.

exam.q: Name the liquid that passes through the filter paper during filtration.
model: Filtrate
exam.tip: Don't mix up filtrate and residue.

exam.q: Explain why filtration can separate sand from salt solution.
model: Sand is insoluble / does not dissolve so its grains are trapped by the filter paper
Salt is dissolved so it passes through with the water (in the filtrate)
exam.tip: Refer to solubility of each substance.

exam.q: State why water enters a Liebig condenser at the bottom.
model: So the condenser fills completely with water / for more efficient cooling
exam.tip: 'Keeps it full' is the key idea.

exam.q: Describe how to obtain pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate from copper sulfate solution.
model: Heat the solution in an evaporating basin to evaporate some of the water
Until crystals start to form / solution is saturated (test with glass rod)
Leave to cool so crystals form
Filter off the crystals and dry them between filter paper / in a warm oven
exam.tip: Do not write 'evaporate all the water'.

exam.q: Explain why simple distillation can be used to obtain pure water from sea water.
model: Water has a much lower boiling point than the salt / water boils and turns to vapour, salt stays in the flask
Water vapour is cooled in the condenser and condenses to liquid water
exam.tip: Mention both evaporation and condensation.

exam.q: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C. Explain why fractional distillation, rather than simple distillation, is used to separate them.
model: They are miscible liquids with fairly close boiling points
Fractional distillation gives repeated evaporation and condensation in the column / a temperature gradient so they separate more completely
exam.tip: State which comes off first: ethanol.

exam.q: Describe how fractional distillation separates a mixture of ethanol and water.
model: Heat the mixture; both liquids evaporate and vapours rise up the fractionating column
The column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top
Water (higher b.p.) condenses and drips back; ethanol (lower b.p.) vapour reaches the top
Ethanol is condensed in the condenser and collected while the temperature stays at about 78 °C; change beaker when temperature rises
exam.tip: Always mention the temperature gradient.

exam.q: Give one safety precaution when distilling a mixture containing ethanol.
model: Use an electric heater / water bath instead of a Bunsen flame because ethanol is flammable (or eye protection, anti-bumping granules)
exam.tip: Link the precaution to the hazard.

exam.q: Rock salt is a mixture of sodium chloride and sand. Describe and explain how a student could obtain pure, dry sodium chloride crystals from rock salt.
model: Grind the rock salt and add (warm) water, stirring to dissolve the sodium chloride
Sodium chloride is soluble but sand is insoluble
Filter: sand is left as the residue, salt solution is the filtrate
Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to evaporate some of the water until crystals begin to form
Leave to cool so sodium chloride crystals form
Filter / pat dry with filter paper or leave in a warm place to dry the crystals
exam.tip: Name each step AND the property it relies on.

exam.q: A mixture contains three miscible liquids: A (b.p. 56 °C), B (b.p. 82 °C) and C (b.p. 118 °C). State the order in which they distil and explain how a student knows when to change the collecting beaker.
model: Order: A, then B, then C
Lowest boiling point reaches the top of the column / condenser first
Thermometer reading stays constant (at 56 °C) while A distils
When the temperature rises (towards 82 °C) A has finished, so change the beaker; repeat for B
exam.tip: Use the thermometer reading as evidence.

worked.q: Choose and justify a method to separate each mixture: (a) chalk powder and water, (b) pure water from blue ink, (c) the colours in a sweet coating, (d) petrol and diesel from crude oil.
steps: (a) Chalk is insoluble in water -> filtration; chalk is the residue
(b) The water has a much lower boiling point than the dyes -> simple distillation; water collected as distillate
(c) The dyes are soluble and have different solubility / attraction to paper -> paper chromatography
(d) Petrol and diesel are miscible liquids with different boiling points -> fractional distillation
worked.ans: (a) filtration, (b) simple distillation, (c) paper chromatography, (d) fractional distillation.

worked.q: A student adds excess insoluble copper oxide to warm sulfuric acid to make copper sulfate solution. Plan how to obtain pure dry copper sulfate crystals.
steps: Unreacted copper oxide is an insoluble solid; copper sulfate is dissolved
Filter the mixture: excess copper oxide is the residue, copper sulfate solution is the filtrate
Pour the filtrate into an evaporating basin and heat gently to evaporate some water
Stop when crystals appear on a glass rod dipped in and removed (saturated)
Leave to cool slowly so crystals form, then filter them off
Dry the crystals between filter papers (not by strong heating, which would remove water of crystallisation)
worked.ans: Filter off excess copper oxide, crystallise copper sulfate from the filtrate by partial evaporation and cooling, then filter and dry the crystals.

worked.q: During fractional distillation of a mixture, the thermometer reads 65 °C for 10 minutes, then rises quickly to 100 °C and stays there. Methanol boils at 65 °C. Interpret these results.
steps: A constant reading means one pure substance is distilling
At 65 °C methanol (lowest b.p.) is reaching the condenser and being collected
The quick rise shows the methanol has all distilled over
The new steady reading of 100 °C matches the boiling point of water
So the second liquid is water, and the beaker should be changed when the temperature rises
worked.ans: The mixture was methanol and water; methanol distilled first at 65 °C, then water at 100 °C.

chem_edx.2.3.summary: Paper chromatography separates a mixture of soluble substances by letting a solvent (the **mobile phase**) soak up through paper (which holds the **stationary phase**). Each substance spends a different amount of time dissolved in the moving solvent versus stuck to the paper, so they travel different distances and form separate spots on a **chromatogram**. You can use the chromatogram to tell pure from impure substances, to identify substances by comparing them with known reference substances, and to identify them by calculating **Rf values**.

core.p: Paper chromatography is a separation technique for mixtures of **soluble** substances, such as the dyes in an ink or food colouring. A solvent moves up the paper and carries the substances with it, but each one moves a different distance, so they separate.
bullets: Used for small amounts of **soluble, coloured** (or detectable) substances.
A **solvent (the mobile phase)** runs through the mixture on the paper.
The **paper contains the stationary phase**, which does not move.
Different substances move **different distances** over the paper, so they separate into spots.
The finished paper with its pattern of spots is called a **chromatogram**.

callouts.p: The separation of mixtures of soluble substances by running a solvent (mobile phase) through the mixture on the paper (the paper contains the stationary phase), which causes the substances to move different distances over the paper.

core.p: Every type of chromatography has two phases. Understanding which is which is the key to explaining WHY substances separate.
bullets: **Mobile phase** = the solvent (for example water or ethanol). It moves up the paper by soaking through it.
**Stationary phase** = held in the paper. It stays still.
Each substance is shared (distributed) between the two phases.
A substance can only move forwards while it is **dissolved in the mobile phase**.
When it is attracted to the stationary phase it is held back.

callouts.p: Solvent = mobile phase. Paper = contains the stationary phase. Swapping these loses the mark.

core.p: Substances separate because they have different balances between how **soluble** they are in the solvent and how strongly they are **attracted to the paper**.
bullets: A substance that is **more soluble in the solvent** spends more time in the mobile phase, so it **moves further** up the paper.
A substance that is **more strongly attracted to the stationary phase** spends more time stuck to the paper, so it **moves a shorter distance**.
Because each substance has its own balance, each travels its own distance in the same time, so the spots separate.
A substance that is **insoluble** in the solvent does not move at all and stays on the baseline.
Changing the solvent changes the solubilities, so the spots can end up in different positions.

callouts.p: Always link solubility to distance: more soluble in the mobile phase means further travelled; more attracted to the stationary phase means less far travelled.

core.p: The method is simple, but every step has a reason that examiners like to ask about.
bullets: Draw a **baseline in pencil** about 1 to 2 cm from the bottom of the paper.
Put **small, concentrated spots** of each sample on the baseline, spaced apart.
Pour solvent into a beaker to a depth **below the baseline**.
Hang the paper so the bottom dips into the solvent but the **spots stay above the solvent**.
Put a **lid** on the beaker.
Leave until the solvent has nearly reached the top, then remove the paper.
Immediately mark the **solvent front** in pencil, then let the paper dry.

core.p: Many marks come from explaining the precautions rather than just listing them.
bullets: **Pencil, not pen**: graphite is insoluble so it will not move; ink would dissolve and run, adding extra spots.
**Baseline above the solvent**: otherwise the samples dissolve into the solvent in the beaker instead of moving up the paper.
**Small, concentrated spots**: give neat, separate spots that do not smear into each other.
**Lid on**: keeps the air saturated with solvent vapour and stops the solvent evaporating from the paper.
**Mark the solvent front straight away**: it becomes invisible once the solvent evaporates, and you need it for Rf values.
**Stop before the solvent reaches the top**: otherwise you cannot measure how far the solvent travelled.

callouts.p: Saying the solvent must be 'below the paper' is wrong. The paper must dip into the solvent; it is the baseline and spots that must stay above it.

core.p: A chromatogram can show whether a substance is pure (one substance only) or a mixture.
bullets: A **pure substance** gives **one spot** on the chromatogram.
A **mixture (impure substance)** gives **two or more spots**, one for each soluble component.
A pure substance gives one spot in **every** solvent tried.
Two substances could have the same Rf in one solvent, so a single spot in one solvent strongly suggests, but does not prove, purity. Running in a second solvent is better evidence.
A spot left on the baseline is an **insoluble** component, so it still counts as a component of the mixture.

callouts.p: Pure substance: one spot. Mixture: more than one spot.

core.p: You can identify the substances in an unknown mixture by running it alongside known reference substances on the same paper with the same solvent.
bullets: Spot the unknown and several **known reference substances** on the same baseline.
Run them at the same time, in the **same solvent**, on the **same paper**.
If a spot from the unknown is at the **same height** as a reference spot, it is likely to be that substance.
If no reference matches a spot, the unknown contains a substance not among the references.
Using the same paper and solvent means conditions are identical, so the comparison is fair.

fig.cap: Comparing unknown X with known substances A, B and C. X has spots level with A and C, so X contains A and C but not B. Each reference gives a single spot.

core.p: The **Rf value** (retention factor) is a number that describes how far a substance moves compared with the solvent. It lets you identify substances without running references on the same paper.
bullets: Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent
Measure **both distances from the baseline**.
Measure to the **centre of the spot** and to the **solvent front**.
Use the same units for both distances; they cancel, so **Rf has no units**.
Rf is always **between 0 and 1**, because a substance can never travel further than the solvent.
An insoluble substance that stays on the baseline has Rf = 0.

callouts.p: Rf = distance moved by substance (spot) / distance moved by solvent (solvent front), both measured from the baseline.
If your Rf comes out bigger than 1, you have divided the wrong way round.

core.p: Under the **same conditions** a substance always has the **same Rf value**, so Rf values can be looked up in a data table to identify unknowns.
bullets: Calculate the Rf of each spot in the unknown.
Compare with a table of known Rf values measured **in the same solvent** and conditions.
A matching Rf suggests the identity of the substance.
Rf depends on the **solvent**, the **type of paper** and the **temperature**, so Rf values from different solvents cannot be compared.
Matching Rf values in **two different solvents** gives much stronger evidence of identity.

callouts.p: Distances depend on how long you leave the paper; the ratio does not, so Rf can be compared between experiments.

core.p: Here is a measured chromatogram. Work through the measurements exactly as in the exam: baseline to spot centre, baseline to solvent front.
bullets: Solvent front is 8.0 cm from the baseline.
Spot A centre is 6.0 cm from the baseline, so Rf = 6.0 / 8.0 = 0.75.
Spot B centre is 2.0 cm from the baseline, so Rf = 2.0 / 8.0 = 0.25.
Spot A is more soluble in the solvent than spot B (or less attracted to the paper).
Give Rf to 2 decimal places unless told otherwise.

core.p: When given any chromatogram in the exam, work through the same set of questions.
bullets: How many spots in the sample? That is the minimum number of soluble components.
Is there a spot on the baseline? That is an insoluble substance.
Which spots line up with reference substances?
Which spot moved furthest? It is the most soluble in the solvent.
Are any spots unmatched? Those are substances not in the reference set.
Could two substances be hiding in one spot? Suggest using a different solvent.

callouts.p: Spots show the minimum number of components: two substances with the same Rf in this solvent would appear as one spot.

analogy.t: A crowd walking up a moving walkway lined with shops
analogy.p: Imagine people stepping onto a moving walkway (the solvent, the mobile phase). The walls are lined with shops (the paper, the stationary phase). People who love shopping keep stepping off to browse, so they get carried only a short way; people who ignore the shops stay on the walkway and get carried far. After a fixed time, everyone has spread out by how much they like shopping, just as substances spread out by their balance of solubility and attraction to the paper. The Rf value is like the fraction of the walkway each person covered. Where it breaks down: real molecules do not choose anything; they constantly dissolve and stick and redissolve millions of times because of attractive forces, and the walkway itself (solvent) slows down as it climbs the paper.

terms.d: Separation of mixtures of soluble substances by running a solvent through the mixture on paper so the substances move different distances.
The phase that moves; in paper chromatography it is the solvent.
The phase that does not move; it is contained in the paper.
The liquid that dissolves the substances and carries them up the paper.
The pattern of separated spots produced on the paper after chromatography.
The pencil line near the bottom of the paper on which samples are spotted; distances are measured from it.
The furthest point the solvent reaches up the paper, marked in pencil when the paper is removed.
Distance moved by substance divided by distance moved by solvent, both measured from the baseline; between 0 and 1 with no units.
A single element or compound not mixed with anything else; gives one spot on a chromatogram.
Two or more substances not chemically combined; gives more than one spot.
Able to dissolve in a particular solvent.
Unable to dissolve in a particular solvent; an insoluble substance stays on the baseline.
A known substance run alongside an unknown so spots can be compared.
One of the separate substances that make up a mixture.

mistakes.w: The paper is the mobile phase and the solvent is stationary.
mistakes.r: The solvent is the mobile phase; the paper contains the stationary phase.

mistakes.w: Draw the baseline in pen so it is easy to see.
mistakes.r: Use pencil because graphite is insoluble and will not run; ink would dissolve and separate.

mistakes.w: Put the solvent above the baseline so the spots dissolve.
mistakes.r: The solvent must be below the baseline, otherwise the samples dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.

mistakes.w: Rf = distance moved by solvent / distance moved by substance.
mistakes.r: Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent, so it is always less than 1.

mistakes.w: Measuring from the bottom edge of the paper.
mistakes.r: Both distances are measured from the baseline, to the centre of the spot and to the solvent front.

mistakes.w: Giving Rf with units such as cm.
mistakes.r: Rf is a ratio of two distances, so it has no units.

mistakes.w: The spot that moves furthest is the heaviest or least soluble.
mistakes.r: The spot that moves furthest is the most soluble in the solvent / least attracted to the stationary phase.

mistakes.w: A spot on the baseline means the substance is pure.
mistakes.r: A spot on the baseline is a substance that is insoluble in that solvent.

mistakes.w: X contains B because it has the same colour.
mistakes.r: Identity is shown by spots at the same height (same Rf) in the same solvent, not colour alone.

exam.q: Name the mobile phase in paper chromatography.
model: The solvent.
exam.tip: One word answer; do not say 'water' unless the question says the solvent is water.

exam.q: Explain why the baseline is drawn in pencil rather than ink.
model: Pencil / graphite is insoluble in the solvent so will not move.
Ink would dissolve and separate, giving extra spots / interfering with results.
exam.tip: Two marks: one for the property of pencil, one for what ink would do.

exam.q: Explain why the solvent level must be below the baseline.
model: Otherwise the samples / spots would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.
So they would not travel up the paper / no chromatogram forms.
exam.tip: Talk about the samples dissolving into the bulk solvent.

exam.q: A spot moved 3.6 cm and the solvent front moved 9.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value.
model: = 0.40 (no units)
exam.tip: Show the division; correct answer alone usually gets full marks but working protects you.

exam.q: State how a chromatogram shows that a food colouring is a mixture.
model: It produces more than one spot.
exam.tip: A pure substance gives a single spot.

exam.q: A sample of ink X and dyes A, B and C were run on the same paper. X gave spots at the same heights as A and C. What can you conclude?
model: X contains A and C.
X does not contain B.
exam.tip: Give both what is present and what is absent.

exam.q: Explain why one dye moves further up the paper than another.
model: It is more soluble in the solvent / mobile phase.
It is less strongly attracted to the paper / stationary phase so spends more time in the mobile phase.
exam.tip: Use the words mobile phase and stationary phase.

exam.q: One spot from a mixture stayed on the baseline. Explain what this shows and suggest how to make it move.
model: The substance is insoluble in the solvent used.
Repeat using a different solvent in which it is soluble.
exam.tip: Insoluble, not 'heavy'.

exam.q: A student says a substance must be pure because it gave one spot. Evaluate this claim.
model: One spot suggests it is pure / only one soluble substance present.
But two substances could have the same Rf in that solvent, so repeat in a different solvent; one spot again gives stronger evidence.
exam.tip: Evaluate means give both sides.

exam.q: Describe how paper chromatography could be used to identify the dyes in a black ink. Include how Rf values are used.
model: Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of chromatography paper.
Put a small spot of the ink and spots of known dyes on the baseline.
Dip the paper in a solvent with the solvent level below the baseline; put a lid on.
Remove before the solvent reaches the top and mark the solvent front in pencil.
Match spots in the ink to spots of known dyes at the same height.
Measure from the baseline to each spot centre and to the solvent front; Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent.
Compare Rf values with a table of known values measured in the same solvent to identify dyes.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a logical order: set-up, running, measuring, interpreting.

exam.q: Explain why Rf values can be compared between experiments but distances moved cannot.
model: Distances depend on how long the chromatogram runs / how far the solvent travels.
Rf is a ratio of distances so it stays the same for a substance in the same solvent and conditions.
exam.tip: Mention same solvent / conditions.

worked.q: On a chromatogram the solvent front is 8.0 cm from the baseline. Spot A is 6.0 cm and spot B is 2.0 cm from the baseline. Calculate both Rf values and say which dye is more soluble in the solvent.
steps: Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent.
A has the larger Rf so it moved further, so it is more soluble in the solvent (less attracted to the paper).
worked.ans: Rf of A = 0.75, Rf of B = 0.25; A is more soluble in the solvent.

worked.q: A dye in an unknown sample moved 4.2 cm when the solvent moved 6.0 cm. Data table (same solvent): Dye P Rf 0.45, Dye Q Rf 0.70, Dye R Rf 0.85. Identify the dye.
steps: Compare with the table: 0.70 matches dye Q.
The table was measured in the same solvent, so the comparison is valid.

worked.q: Spot C has an Rf of 0.30. The solvent front moved 7.5 cm. How far did spot C travel from the baseline?
steps: Rearrange: distance moved by substance = Rf x distance moved by solvent.
Distance = 0.30 x 7.5.
Distance = 2.25 cm.

chem_edx.2.4.summary: In this core practical you investigate what an ink is made of in two parts. **Simple distillation** separates the **solvent** from the ink: the solvent boils off, is condensed and collected, and its **boiling point** (read on the thermometer) identifies it, for example 100 °C shows it is water. **Paper chromatography** then separates the **coloured dyes** in the ink so you can count them and identify them by comparison with known dyes or by their **Rf values**.

core.p: Ink is a **mixture**: a solvent (often water) with one or more dissolved **dyes**. No single technique can investigate both parts, so two methods are used.
bullets: **Simple distillation** separates and identifies the **solvent** in the ink.
**Paper chromatography** separates and identifies the **dyes** in the ink.
Distillation works because the solvent has a much **lower boiling point** than the dyes.
Chromatography works because the dyes have different **solubilities** in the chromatography solvent and different attractions to the paper.
Together they tell you the full composition of the ink.

core.p: Simple distillation separates a **liquid (the solvent) from a solution**, leaving the dissolved dyes behind.
bullets: Put about 20 to 30 cm3 of ink into a **round-bottomed or distillation flask** and add a few **anti-bumping granules**.
Fit a **thermometer** so that its bulb is level with the **side arm** leading to the condenser.
Connect the side arm to a **Liebig condenser** with cold water going **in at the bottom** and **out at the top**.
Place a beaker or test tube at the end of the condenser to collect the **distillate**; standing it in iced water helps condensation.
**Heat gently** with a Bunsen burner (or electric heater) until the ink boils.
Record the **temperature when it stays constant** while liquid drips into the collecting vessel.
Stop heating before the flask boils dry.

core.h: Why each piece of apparatus is set up that way
core.p: Examiners regularly ask you to explain the details of the distillation set-up.
bullets: **Thermometer bulb at the side arm**: it measures the temperature of the **vapour** that is leaving to be condensed, which is the boiling point of the substance being collected.
**Water in at the bottom, out at the top**: the condenser fills completely with cold water, so it cools the vapour most efficiently.
**Condenser**: cold surface turns the vapour back into liquid (condensation).
**Anti-bumping granules**: give smooth boiling and stop sudden violent bubbling.
**Iced water around the collecting tube**: makes sure all the vapour condenses and reduces loss by evaporation.
**Do not heat to dryness**: the flask could crack and the dye residue could decompose.

callouts.p: If the bulb is down in the liquid it reads the temperature of the boiling mixture, not of the vapour being collected.

core.h: Identifying the solvent from its boiling point
core.p: A **pure substance has a fixed, sharp boiling point**, so the steady temperature recorded during distillation identifies the solvent.
bullets: If the temperature stays at about **100 °C**, the solvent is **water**.
Ethanol would boil at about **78 °C**.
The distillate is **colourless**, showing that the dyes have **not** distilled over.
The dyes have much higher boiling points (or decompose), so they stay in the flask and become more concentrated.
A temperature slightly different from 100 °C can be due to thermometer error or air pressure, not necessarily a different solvent.

callouts.p: Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution because the solvent has a much lower boiling point than the dissolved substances.

core.p: A risk assessment is part of every core practical.
bullets: Wear **eye protection**: hot liquid can spit.
**Heat gently** and use anti-bumping granules to avoid bumping.
Make sure condenser water is flowing before heating.
If the ink solvent could be **flammable** (such as an alcohol), use an electric heater or water bath, not a naked flame.
Do not touch the hot flask; let apparatus cool before taking it apart.
Never heat a completely sealed apparatus: the end of the condenser must be open so pressure cannot build up.

callouts.p: In 'suggest a safety precaution' questions, link the precaution to a specific hazard, for example 'eye protection because hot liquid may spit'.

core.p: Chromatography separates the dyes in the ink so you can see how many there are and what they are.
bullets: Draw a **pencil baseline** about 1.5 cm from the bottom of chromatography paper.
Put a **small spot of the ink** on the baseline, and spots of **known dyes** beside it.
Pour **water** (or another solvent) into a beaker to a depth **below the baseline**.
Hang the paper so the bottom dips into the solvent; put a **lid** on.
Leave until the solvent is near the top, then remove the paper and **mark the solvent front** in pencil.
Allow to dry; measure the distances and calculate **Rf values**.

core.p: The same reasons come up again and again in mark schemes.
bullets: **Pencil baseline**: graphite is insoluble and will not run.
**Baseline above solvent**: so the ink does not dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.
**Small spots**: so the dyes separate cleanly without smearing.
**Lid**: stops the solvent evaporating from the paper.
**Mark solvent front at once**: it vanishes as the paper dries.
**Same paper and solvent for ink and known dyes**: makes the comparison fair.

callouts.p: Measure only after marking the solvent front; once it dries you cannot find it and cannot calculate Rf.

core.p: The chromatogram tells you how many dyes are in the ink and, by comparison, which ones.
bullets: The **number of spots** from the ink = the minimum number of soluble dyes.
Ink spots **level with known dye spots** show which dyes are present.
Calculate **Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent**, both from the baseline.
Compare Rf values with data measured in the **same solvent**.
A spot on the baseline is a dye that is **insoluble** in the solvent used; try another solvent.

fig.cap: Chromatogram of a black ink run beside known dyes. The ink separates into three spots, matching the red, blue and yellow dyes, so black ink is a mixture of at least three dyes.
