core.p: Even a separation practical has variables that must be controlled so results are valid and can be compared.
bullets: Use the **same solvent** for all samples on a chromatogram (Rf depends on the solvent).
Use the **same type of paper** and run at the same **temperature**.
Put all spots on the **same baseline** so they all start at the same point.
Use similar **spot sizes** so spots are easy to compare.
In distillation, record the temperature only once it is **steady**, when the distillate is being collected.

core.p: Evaluation questions ask what could go wrong and how to fix it.
bullets: **Spots smeared or merged**: spots too large or too concentrated; use smaller spots and let each dry before re-spotting.
**Dye stayed on baseline**: insoluble in water; repeat with a different solvent such as ethanol.
**Two dyes in one spot**: they have the same Rf in that solvent; repeat in a different solvent.
**Distillate coloured**: heated too strongly so liquid splashed over; heat more gently.
**Low thermometer reading**: bulb below the side arm or heating not yet steady.
**Low yield of distillate**: poor cooling; check condenser water flow and use iced water.

callouts.p: 'Be more careful' never scores. Name the change and say why it helps.

core.p: Set results out clearly so conclusions follow logically.
bullets: Distillation: record the **steady boiling temperature** and the **appearance** of the distillate and residue.
Chromatography: record distance moved by solvent, distance moved by each spot, and the **calculated Rf** to 2 decimal places.
State the conclusion: what the solvent is, how many dyes, which dyes.
Keep the dried chromatogram as evidence.

analogy.p: Imagine you want to know what is in a cola. You could boil it gently and catch the steam on a cold plate: the clear water you collect is like the distillate, and the sticky brown syrup left behind is like the dye residue. Then, to find out which flavourings and colours make up that syrup, you would need a different, finer test, just as chromatography splits the dyes. Where it breaks down: in the cola some flavourings would also evaporate, whereas in ink the dyes stay behind; and chromatography does not use heat at all, it relies on different solubilities.

terms.d: A mixture of a solvent and one or more dissolved dyes.
The liquid in which other substances are dissolved; in many inks it is water.
A coloured substance dissolved in the ink.
A method to separate a liquid from a solution by evaporating the liquid and then condensing it.
The liquid collected after it has been evaporated and condensed.
What is left in the flask after the solvent has distilled off; here the concentrated dyes.
The temperature at which a liquid boils; a pure substance has a fixed boiling point.
A glass tube with a cold water jacket that cools vapour so it condenses.
The change of state from gas to liquid.
Small pieces added to a liquid to give smooth boiling.
Separation of soluble substances by running a solvent through the mixture on paper, so they move different distances.
The solvent that moves through the paper.
Contained in the paper; does not move.
Distance moved by substance divided by distance moved by solvent, both from the baseline.
The furthest point reached by the solvent on the paper.

mistakes.w: Chromatography is used to find out what the solvent in the ink is.
mistakes.r: Simple distillation identifies the solvent from its boiling point; chromatography separates the dyes.

mistakes.w: The thermometer bulb goes in the ink.
mistakes.r: The bulb is level with the side arm to measure the temperature of the vapour being collected.

mistakes.w: Water goes in at the top of the condenser.
mistakes.r: Water goes in at the bottom and out at the top so the jacket is always full of cold water.

mistakes.w: The distillate is coloured because the dyes evaporate.
mistakes.r: The distillate is colourless; the dyes remain in the flask.

mistakes.w: The condenser heats the vapour.
mistakes.r: The condenser cools the vapour so it condenses into a liquid.

mistakes.w: The temperature was 100 °C so the ink is pure water.
mistakes.r: The solvent is water; the ink is a mixture of water and dyes.

mistakes.w: Draw the baseline in ink so you can see it.
mistakes.r: Draw it in pencil, which is insoluble and will not run.

mistakes.w: Improve by being more careful with the spots.
mistakes.r: Use smaller spots and let each dry, or use a different solvent, with the reason.

exam.q: Name the technique used to obtain the solvent from an ink.
model: Simple distillation.
exam.tip: Not fractional distillation; that is for mixtures of liquids with similar boiling points.

exam.q: State the boiling point reading that shows the solvent in an ink is water.
exam.tip: Include units.

exam.q: Explain why the thermometer bulb is placed next to the side arm of the flask.
model: To measure the temperature of the vapour going into the condenser.
This is the boiling point of the substance being collected / distilled.
exam.tip: Mention vapour.

exam.q: Explain why cold water enters the condenser at the bottom.
model: So the condenser jacket fills completely with water.
This gives more efficient cooling / condensation of the vapour.
exam.tip: 'It works better' is too vague.

exam.q: Explain why the distillate collected from ink is colourless.
model: The dyes have much higher boiling points than the solvent / do not evaporate.
So only the solvent evaporates and is condensed; the dyes stay in the flask.
exam.tip: Link to boiling points.

exam.q: Give one safety precaution when distilling ink and explain it.
model: Wear eye protection / heat gently / use anti-bumping granules / do not heat to dryness.
Because hot liquid may spit or bump / the flask may crack.
exam.tip: Precaution plus reason.

exam.q: The ink gave three spots and one remained on the baseline. What does this tell you?
model: The ink contains at least four dyes / is a mixture.
One dye is insoluble in the solvent used.
exam.tip: Count the baseline spot as a component.

exam.q: A blue dye moved 2.7 cm and the solvent moved 9.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value.
exam.tip: No units.

exam.q: Suggest why a student might repeat the chromatography using ethanol instead of water.
model: A dye did not move / was insoluble in water, or two dyes did not separate.
Dyes have different solubilities in ethanol so may separate / move.
exam.tip: Base the reason on solubility.

exam.q: Describe how a student could investigate the composition of an ink using simple distillation and paper chromatography.
model: Heat ink in a flask with anti-bumping granules; thermometer bulb at side arm.
Vapour passes through a Liebig condenser with cold water in at the bottom; collect the distillate.
Record the steady temperature; 100 °C shows the solvent is water.
Draw a pencil baseline on chromatography paper; spot ink and known dyes on it.
Stand in solvent below the baseline with a lid; remove and mark the solvent front.
Number of spots shows number of dyes; match heights with known dyes / calculate Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent and compare with data.
exam.tip: Cover both techniques and say what each one tells you.

exam.q: During distillation the thermometer read 96 °C. Suggest two reasons.
model: Thermometer not calibrated / inaccurate, or bulb not at the side arm.
Reading taken before the temperature had become steady / lower air pressure.
exam.tip: Do not assume a different solvent if 96 is close to 100.

worked.q: A student distils 25 cm3 of a blue ink. The temperature rises and stays at 100 °C while a colourless liquid collects. A dark blue residue is left. Write a conclusion.
steps: A steady temperature means a pure substance is distilling over.
The boiling point of the collected liquid is 100 °C, the boiling point of water.
The distillate is colourless so the dyes did not distil over.
The dark residue is the dyes, more concentrated because solvent was removed.
worked.ans: The solvent in the ink is water; the blue dye(s) remain in the flask because they have much higher boiling points.

worked.q: On a chromatogram, the solvent front is 8.0 cm from the baseline. The ink gives spots at 6.8 cm, 4.2 cm and 1.8 cm. Known Rf values in water: yellow 0.85, red 0.53, green 0.40, blue 0.22. Identify the dyes.
steps: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent.
6.8 / 8.0 = 0.85, matches yellow.
No spot has Rf 0.40, so green is absent.
worked.ans: The ink contains yellow, red and blue dyes, and no green dye.

worked.q: A student's chromatogram has a large smudged spot and the distillate is pale blue. Explain the problems and suggest improvements.
steps: Smudged spot: the spot was too big / too much ink, so dyes overlapped.
Improve: use a fine capillary tube to make a small spot and let it dry before adding more.
Pale blue distillate: the ink was heated too strongly so it splashed or bumped over into the condenser.
Improve: heat gently and add anti-bumping granules.
worked.ans: Use smaller, dried spots and heat the ink gently with anti-bumping granules.

chem_edx.2.5.summary: **Potable water** is water that is safe to drink; it is not chemically pure because it still contains small amounts of dissolved salts. Ground water and waste water are made potable by **sedimentation** (large insoluble bits settle out), **filtration** through sand and gravel (smaller insoluble particles removed) and **chlorination** (kills harmful microorganisms). Sea water contains too much dissolved salt to drink, so it can be made potable by **simple distillation**, which works but needs lots of energy. Water used in chemical analysis must contain **no dissolved salts**, so distilled or deionised water is used to avoid contaminating results.

core.h: Potable water is not pure water
core.p: In chemistry a **pure substance** contains only one substance. Drinking water is safe but is a **mixture**: water plus small amounts of dissolved salts and gases.
bullets: **Potable water** = water that is **safe to drink**.
It must have **low levels of dissolved salts** and **no harmful microorganisms**.
It still contains some dissolved substances, so it is **not pure** in the chemical sense.
Pure water would boil at exactly 100 °C and freeze at exactly 0 °C; tap water does not quite.
In everyday language 'pure' means clean; in chemistry it means a single substance.

callouts.p: Water that is safe to drink.
Never write that potable water is pure water. It contains dissolved substances.

core.p: The method used to make water potable depends on where it comes from and what is in it.
bullets: **Ground water**: rain that has soaked into rocks (aquifers); usually fairly clean but can contain dissolved substances and some microorganisms.
**Surface water**: lakes, rivers and reservoirs; contains soil, leaves and microorganisms.
**Waste water**: from homes, farms and industry (including sewage); contains much more dirt, organic matter and microorganisms, so needs more treatment.
**Sea water**: contains a high concentration of dissolved salts, which sedimentation and filtration cannot remove.
In the UK most drinking water comes from ground water and surface water.

core.p: Ground water and waste water are made potable in three main stages. Each stage removes a different kind of impurity, which is why all three are needed.
bullets: **Sedimentation**: large insoluble particles settle to the bottom.
**Filtration**: smaller insoluble particles are removed by beds of sand and gravel.
**Chlorination**: chlorine is added to kill microorganisms.
The order matters: removing solids first lets chlorine reach and kill microbes effectively.
None of these stages removes dissolved salts.

callouts.p: Sedimentation, then filtration, then chlorination.

core.p: Water is left to stand in large **sedimentation tanks**. Gravity does the work.
bullets: Large **insoluble** particles such as grit, sand and soil are **denser than water**, so they **sink** to the bottom.
The cleaner water above is then removed for the next stage.
It is cheap because it needs almost no energy, just time.
It cannot remove very small particles, dissolved substances or microorganisms.
Removing most solids first stops the filters clogging quickly.

core.p: The water passes through **filter beds** of **sand and gravel**, which trap smaller insoluble particles that did not settle.
bullets: Gravel at the bottom supports the sand; the fine sand traps tiny particles.
Removes **small insoluble particles** that are too light to settle.
It works because the gaps between sand grains are too small for the particles to pass, but water can flow through.
It does **not** remove dissolved salts, because dissolved ions are far smaller than the gaps.
It does not reliably remove all microorganisms, which is why chlorination follows.

callouts.p: Filtration only removes insoluble solids. Dissolved salt passes straight through.

core.p: Even clear water can contain harmful **microorganisms** (such as bacteria) that cause diseases. **Chlorine** is added to kill them.
bullets: Chlorination **kills microorganisms / bacteria**, making the water safe to drink.
It is done **last**, after solids are removed, so microbes cannot hide inside particles.
A small amount of chlorine stays in the water to keep it safe as it travels through pipes.
Too much chlorine is harmful and tastes unpleasant, so the dose is carefully controlled.
Chlorine does not remove insoluble or dissolved substances; it only sterilises.

callouts.p: Chlorine is added to kill microorganisms (bacteria). It does not 'clean out' dirt or salt.

core.p: Waste water, such as sewage, is much dirtier than ground water, so it must be treated more thoroughly before it can be made potable.
bullets: It contains much more **insoluble solid**, **organic matter** and **microorganisms**.
It can also contain harmful chemicals from industry or farms.
Sedimentation, filtration and chlorination are still needed, but extra treatment is used first.
This makes treating waste water more costly than treating ground water.
Ground water is usually the easiest source to make potable because rocks have already filtered it.

core.h: Making sea water potable by simple distillation
core.p: Sea water contains a high concentration of **dissolved salts** (mainly sodium chloride). Drinking it makes you more dehydrated, and sedimentation, filtration and chlorination cannot remove dissolved salts. **Simple distillation** can.
bullets: Sea water is **heated** so the water **boils** and turns to **steam**.
The salts have very high boiling points, so they **stay behind**.
The steam is **cooled in a condenser** and **condenses** back into liquid water.
The **distillate** has almost no dissolved salts, so it is potable (chlorine may still be added).
This separation works because water has a much **lower boiling point** than the dissolved salts.

callouts.p: For full marks, say water boils / evaporates but the salts do not, then the steam condenses.

core.h: Pros and cons of distilling sea water
core.p: Distillation produces very pure water, but it is not the main method in countries with plenty of fresh water. The reason is energy.
bullets: **Advantage**: removes dissolved salts, which other methods cannot; gives water with very low salt levels.
**Advantage**: useful in dry countries with little fresh water but access to the sea.
**Disadvantage**: boiling large volumes of water needs **huge amounts of energy**, so it is **expensive**.
**Disadvantage**: if the energy comes from burning fossil fuels it releases carbon dioxide.
It is mainly used where fresh water is scarce and energy is relatively cheap.

core.p: When you test or analyse substances in the lab, the water you use must **not contain any dissolved salts**.
bullets: Tap water contains dissolved ions such as chloride, sulfate, calcium and sodium ions.
These ions could **react** with the chemicals in a test or **interfere** with the result.
They could give a **false positive**, for example chloride ions in tap water would give a white precipitate with silver nitrate.
In chromatography or other analysis, extra dissolved substances could appear as **contaminants**.
So analysis uses **distilled water** or **deionised water**, which has had the dissolved salts removed.

callouts.p: Dissolved salts in the water would contaminate the sample and could react or give misleading results.

core.p: Be clear about which kind of water is which, because questions often ask you to choose.
bullets: **Tap (potable) water**: safe to drink, contains some dissolved salts and chlorine; not for analysis.
**Distilled water**: made by distillation; dissolved salts removed; suitable for analysis.
**Deionised water**: dissolved ions removed (by ion exchange); suitable for analysis.
**Sea water**: high levels of dissolved salts; not potable until distilled.
**Ground water**: may contain insoluble particles and microbes; must be treated.

analogy.t: Getting a muddy, salty football kit clean
analogy.p: Making water potable is like cleaning a filthy kit. First you let the big lumps of mud drop off in a bucket (sedimentation), then you rinse it through a sieve-like mesh that catches the fine grit (filtration), then you use a disinfectant wash to kill the germs (chlorination). But if the kit has been soaked in sea water, the salt has gone into the fabric and none of those steps gets it out; you would need a totally different, energy-hungry method, like boiling the water away and catching the steam (distillation). Where it breaks down: in distillation it is the water that moves away from the salt, not the dirt being removed from the water, and real filters remove particles by size, not by scrubbing.

terms.d: Water that is safe to drink; it contains low levels of dissolved salts and microorganisms.
Water containing no other substances at all; only water molecules.
Water found underground in rocks (aquifers).
Used water from homes, farms and industry, including sewage.
Water from the sea containing a high concentration of dissolved salts.
Leaving water to stand so large insoluble particles sink to the bottom.
Passing water through a filter (beds of sand and gravel) to remove small insoluble particles.
Adding chlorine to water to kill microorganisms.
A tiny living organism such as a bacterium that can cause disease.
Does not dissolve; can be removed by sedimentation or filtration.
An ionic compound that has dissolved in water; cannot be removed by filtration.
Separating a liquid from a solution by boiling the liquid and condensing the vapour.
Change from a gas to a liquid on cooling.
Removing dissolved salts from sea water, for example by distillation.
Water that has been purified by distillation so it contains almost no dissolved salts.
Water from which dissolved ions have been removed.

mistakes.w: Potable water is pure water.
mistakes.r: Potable water is safe to drink but contains dissolved substances, so it is not pure.

mistakes.w: Filtration removes the salt from sea water.
mistakes.r: Filtration removes only insoluble particles; dissolved salts pass through. Distillation is needed.

mistakes.w: Chlorine is added to remove dirt.
mistakes.r: Chlorine is added to kill microorganisms / bacteria.

mistakes.w: Sedimentation kills bacteria.
mistakes.r: Sedimentation lets large insoluble particles settle out.

mistakes.w: Distilling sea water is not used because it does not work.
mistakes.r: It works, but it needs large amounts of energy so it is expensive.

mistakes.w: In distillation the salt evaporates and is collected.
mistakes.r: The water evaporates and is condensed; the salts are left behind.

mistakes.w: Tap water is fine for analysis because it is clean.
mistakes.r: Tap water contains dissolved salts which could react or contaminate results; use distilled or deionised water.

mistakes.w: Chlorination is done first.
mistakes.r: Chlorination is the last stage, after sedimentation and filtration.

exam.q: What is meant by potable water?
model: Water that is safe to drink.
exam.tip: Do not say pure.

exam.q: State why chlorine is added to drinking water.
model: To kill microorganisms / bacteria.
exam.tip: 'Kills germs' is usually accepted but 'bacteria' or 'microorganisms' is safer.

exam.q: Explain why potable water is not pure.
model: It contains dissolved substances / salts.
A pure substance contains only one substance.
exam.tip: Give the chemical meaning of pure.

exam.q: Describe the purpose of sedimentation and filtration in water treatment.
model: Sedimentation: large insoluble particles settle out / sink to the bottom.
Filtration: smaller insoluble particles are removed by sand and gravel beds.
exam.tip: Say 'insoluble' particles.

exam.q: Explain why filtration cannot make sea water potable.
model: The salts in sea water are dissolved.
Dissolved substances pass through a filter; filtration only removes insoluble solids.
exam.tip: Key idea: dissolved versus insoluble.

exam.q: Describe how sea water can be made potable by simple distillation.
model: Heat the sea water so the water boils / evaporates.
The salts do not evaporate / have much higher boiling points and are left behind.
The steam is cooled in a condenser.
It condenses to liquid water, which is collected.
exam.tip: Four steps: boil, salts left, cool, condense and collect.

exam.q: Give one reason why distillation of sea water is not used to produce drinking water in the UK.
model: It needs a lot of energy / is expensive, and the UK has plenty of fresh ground and surface water.
exam.tip: Energy and cost are the key ideas.

exam.q: Explain why water used in chemical analysis must not contain dissolved salts.
model: Dissolved salts / ions would contaminate the sample.
They could react with the test reagents / give a false result.
exam.tip: Give a specific example if you can, such as chloride ions with silver nitrate.

exam.q: Suggest which type of water a technician should use to prepare solutions for testing for chloride ions and explain why.
model: Distilled or deionised water.
Tap water contains chloride ions which would give a white precipitate with silver nitrate / a false positive.
exam.tip: Link the contaminant to the test.

exam.q: Describe and explain how ground water is made potable.
model: Sedimentation: water left to stand in tanks.
Large insoluble particles are denser so sink to the bottom.
Filtration: water passed through beds of sand and gravel.
Removes smaller insoluble particles.
Chlorination: chlorine added.
Kills microorganisms / bacteria so the water is safe to drink; done last so solids do not protect microbes.
exam.tip: For each stage, say what is done and why.

exam.q: Compare making potable water from ground water with making it from sea water.
model: Ground water: sedimentation, filtration and chlorination.
Sea water: simple distillation, to remove dissolved salts.
Treating ground water needs little energy / is cheap.
Distillation needs a lot of energy so is expensive.
exam.tip: Compare means give points for both sides.

worked.q: A country has little rainfall but a long coastline and cheap solar energy. Explain which method it should use to make potable water.
steps: Little rainfall means there is little ground or surface water to treat.
Sea water is available but contains dissolved salts that filtration cannot remove.
Simple distillation removes the dissolved salts by boiling the water and condensing the steam.
Distillation needs a lot of energy, but here energy is cheap, so the main disadvantage is reduced.
worked.ans: Distil sea water: it removes dissolved salts, and cheap solar energy makes the high energy demand affordable.

worked.q: A student tests a sample for sulfate ions using water from the tap to dissolve it. The test gives a white precipitate even though the sample has no sulfate. Explain the result and how to fix it.
steps: Tap water is potable but contains dissolved salts, which can include sulfate ions.
These ions react with the test reagent, giving a white precipitate.
This is a false positive caused by contamination from the water.
Repeat using distilled or deionised water, which contains no dissolved salts.
worked.ans: Dissolved sulfate ions in tap water gave a false positive; use distilled or deionised water.

worked.q: Put these stages in order and explain the order: chlorination, filtration, sedimentation.
steps: Sedimentation first: removes most large insoluble particles cheaply, so filters do not clog.
Filtration second: removes the smaller insoluble particles left behind.
Chlorination last: with solids removed, chlorine can reach and kill all microorganisms.
Some chlorine remains to keep the water safe in the pipes.
